1009.title: Camillus de Lellis (mid-July)
1009.hook: a gambler and soldier who founded nursing brothers with red crosses on their habits
1009.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Camillus de Lellis in mid-July as a patron of the sick, nurses and hospitals, and his order, the Camillians, still serves the sick wearing the red cross.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Our Lady of Mount Carmel and the brown scapular. Your line was under her mantle. What were you carrying on your shoulders? Day one thousand nine.

A young man with a bad leg and a worse habit. He's been a soldier for hire, fighting wherever there's pay. Between wars he plays cards and dice, and he loses. Tradition says he once gambled away nearly everything he owned, down to the shirt on his back. To eat, he takes work as a laborer, then as an attendant in a hospital in Rome, the kind of place for people nobody expects to get well. He's dismissed for gambling. Today, how that man ended up founding an order of nurses.
screen: `A SOLDIER FOR HIRE.` → `CARDS, DICE, AND DEBT.` → `DISMISSED FROM A HOSPITAL.`

segments.voice: Camillus de Lellis didn't turn around all at once. Tradition says the change began while he was working as a laborer for Capuchin friars, when one of them took him aside and spoke to him plainly about his life. He was taken in as a novice, but the wound on his leg, which never healed, opened again, and the friars sent him away. So he went back to the hospital, and this time he stayed. And he watched how the sick were treated. Hired attendants who didn't care. Patients left dirty, hungry, alone. He began to gather a few men who would nurse the sick the way a mother nurses her only child, a picture tradition gives in his own words. That little group became an order, called the Ministers of the Infirm, and Camillus became a priest. The red cross came next. His brothers wore a large red cross on the chest of their black habits, so that anyone, in a ward or a street, could see who had come to serve. They went into hospitals, into the homes of the dying, onto battlefields. Under all of it was the Gospel scene of the last judgment, where Jesus counts care for the sick as care done to himself. For Camillus, that was not a figure of speech: the patient in the bed was Christ. And the old gambler kept something from his past: he never stopped taking risks. He just changed what he bet on.
screen: `A FRIAR SPEAKS PLAINLY.` · `BACK TO THE HOSPITAL, TO STAY.` · `A RED CROSS ON A BLACK HABIT.` · `THE PATIENT IS CHRIST.` · then, large: `HE CHANGED WHAT HE BET ON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember someone who nursed you. Settle, and breathe. Go back to a time you were sick or hurt. A hospital bed, a fever at home, a long recovery. Who took care of you? A nurse whose name you never learned. A parent. A friend who brought soup. Stay with their hands, their voice, what they did that you couldn't do. If you pray, you can thank God for them and ask a blessing on their work. If you don't, simply hold them in gratitude for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Camillus, once a soldier and gambler. He became a priest and gathered brothers to nurse the sick, marked with a red cross on their habits.
Your line: the red cross. Today, do one plain job for someone who is sick or worn out, the kind a hired attendant skips: a fresh glass of water, a changed sheet, a dish washed. Day one thousand nine.

1010.title: Sharbel Makhlouf (24 July)
1010.hook: a Maronite hermit of Lebanon, who kept silence for years
1010.howItsDone: Maronite Catholics and others honor Saint Sharbel, and pilgrims visit his monastery and hermitage in the mountains of Lebanon to pray.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Camillus de Lellis, the gambler who became a nurse to the sick. Your line was the red cross. Which nurse did you thank? Day one thousand ten.

High in the mountains of Lebanon, above a monastery, there is a small stone hermitage. One monk lives there. He rises in the dark to pray. He works the vineyard with his hands. He eats once a day, tradition says, and very little. He speaks only when he must. Visitors who climb up to see him find a man who mostly says nothing at all. He wrote no books that we know of. He gave no famous sermons. And yet today pilgrims crowd the road to that mountain. Today, a saint whose teaching was silence.
screen: `A HERMITAGE IN THE MOUNTAINS.` → `PRAYER, VINES, ONE MEAL.` → `A MAN WHO SAYS NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Sharbel Makhlouf was a monk of the Maronite Church. The Maronites are Eastern Catholics, rooted in Lebanon, in full communion with the pope, with their own ancient liturgy, prayed in part in Syriac, a form of Aramaic, close to the language Jesus spoke. So this is a Catholic saint, and also a saint from a different branch of the Catholic family than some listeners know. He was born with another name and took the name Sharbel when he became a monk. After years in the monastery, he asked to live as a hermit, and he spent the rest of his life in that hermitage, in prayer and silence, for many years, tradition says. Why silence? In the books of Kings, Elijah waits on a mountain for God. A great wind passes, then an earthquake, then fire, and the Lord is not in them. Then, in the Douay-Rheims: "after the fire a whistling of a gentle air." Not in the noise. In the quiet after it. Stories gathered around him even while he lived. Tradition tells of a lamp the other monks filled with water as a test, and it burned anyway. After his death, the stories multiplied, of light seen at his grave, of healings, and pilgrims began to come and still do. The Church examined these claims before naming him a saint. But the heart of it is simple. A man went quiet for God, for years, and that quiet still draws people up a mountain.
screen: `A MONK OF THE MARONITE CHURCH.` · `HE ASKED TO LIVE AS A HERMIT.` · `GOD IN THE QUIET AFTER THE FIRE.` · `QUIET THAT STILL DRAWS PEOPLE.` · then, large: `A WHISTLING OF A GENTLE AIR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep silence, on purpose. Settle, and breathe. For these two minutes, no words, not even in your head if you can help it. When a sentence starts, let it trail off. Hear what's left: the room, the street, your breath. If you pray, you can rest in that gentle air from Elijah's mountain, and let the rest go. If you don't, simply let the quiet be enough. And if you can, after the bell, keep going, and make it five minutes. The bell holds the time.
Sharbel Makhlouf. A Maronite monk of Lebanon who lived his last years as a hermit, in prayer and silence.
Your line: silence of lebanon. Today, find five minutes with no screen, no music, no talk, and keep them. Day one thousand ten.

1011.title: James (25 July)
1011.hook: the apostle honored at Santiago de Compostela, goal of the Camino pilgrimage
1011.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint James the apostle on 25 July, and pilgrims walk the Camino de Santiago, ending at the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sharbel Makhlouf, the hermit of the Lebanese mountains. Your line was silence of lebanon. Did you find five quiet minutes? Day one thousand eleven.

A scallop shell tied to a backpack. A pair of boots gone gray with dust. Yellow arrows painted on walls, on rocks, on the corners of village houses, all pointing the same way. Follow them long enough, through fields and towns and over hills, and they bring you to a great cathedral in the northwest of Spain, in a city called Santiago de Compostela. Santiago means Saint James. The road has a name, too, and pilgrims say it often. Today, James, and the road that carries his name.
screen: `A SHELL ON A BACKPACK.` → `YELLOW ARROWS.` → `A CATHEDRAL IN SPAIN.`

segments.voice: Camino is Spanish for way, or road. The Camino de Santiago is the way of Saint James. But first, the man. James was a fisherman, a son of Zebedee, the brother of John. Jesus called the two of them from their boat and their nets, and they followed. With Peter and John, James was one of the three Jesus took up the mountain of the transfiguration. In Mark's Gospel Jesus gives the brothers a nickname, sons of thunder, and Luke tells a story that fits it: once, when a village turned them away, they offered to call down fire on it. Jesus rebuked them. Then there's the day their mother asks for the best seats in the kingdom for her sons. Jesus turns to the brothers. In the Douay-Rheims: "Can you drink the chalice that I shall drink? They say to him: We can." They had no idea what they were saying yes to. James found out. In the Acts of the Apostles, King Herod has him killed with the sword. The son of thunder died a witness. Then comes tradition. It says James carried the gospel to Spain, and that after his death his body was brought there and later found and honored at Compostela. Historians weigh those stories differently, and the Church keeps them as tradition. But the road grew around the tomb, and pilgrims walk it still, on foot, step after step, toward an apostle who once said, we can, before he knew the cost.
screen: `CAMINO MEANS WAY.` · `A FISHERMAN, A SON OF THUNDER.` · `CAN YOU DRINK THE CHALICE?` · `A ROAD GROWS AROUND A TOMB.` · then, large: `THEY SAY TO HIM: WE CAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk like a pilgrim. If you can, stand up and walk slowly, around the room or down a hallway. Feel each step land. Heel, then the ball of the foot. If you can't walk, let your hands rest on your knees and feel your breath move like steps. Pilgrims walk toward something, so pick one thing you're walking toward this season. If you pray, you can offer each step for it. If you don't, simply let each step be a step. The bell holds the time.
Camino. Spanish for way or road. The Camino de Santiago is the pilgrim road to the tomb of Saint James in Spain.
Your line: the way of saint james. Today, walk a mile as a pilgrim: no headphones, no hurry, with one person or one hope in mind. Day one thousand eleven.

1012.title: Martha, Mary and Lazarus (29 July)
1012.hook: the Bethany family, now celebrated together on one day
1012.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saints Martha, Mary and Lazarus on 29 July, hearing Martha's story from the Gospels of Luke or John at Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, James, the son of thunder, and the long road to his tomb in Spain. Your line was the way of saint james. Where did you walk? Day one thousand twelve.

There's a guest in the house, and the kitchen is chaos. Bread to bake, water to fetch, a meal to get on the table. One sister is doing all of it. The other is sitting in the next room, on the floor, listening. The busy one finally comes out, hands still floured, and says it out loud: tell her to help me. The guest is Jesus. The house is in Bethany, a village near Jerusalem. And the three who live there, two sisters and a brother, are kept together on today's feast. Today's word is the sister in the kitchen.
screen: `A GUEST, A BUSY KITCHEN.` → `ONE SISTER LISTENING.` → `TELL HER TO HELP ME.`

segments.voice: Luke tells the kitchen scene. Martha welcomes Jesus into her house. Mary sits at his feet. Martha, busy with much serving, asks him to send her sister to help. And Jesus answers her gently, saying her name twice. In the Douay-Rheims: "Martha, Martha, thou art careful, and art troubled about many things." Careful here means full of cares. He goes on: one thing is necessary, and Mary has chosen the best part. It's easy to hear that as a scolding. Some readers stop there and side with Martha. But look where the story starts: Martha is the one who opened the door. Without her there's no house, no meal, no place for Mary to sit. Now John's Gospel. Lazarus, their brother, falls sick, and the sisters send word to Jesus. By the time he comes, Lazarus has been in the tomb for days. And who goes out down the road to meet him? Martha. She tells him straight that if he'd been there, her brother wouldn't have died. Then, a few lines later, she says she believes he is the Christ, the Son of God. At the tomb, John writes, "Jesus wept." Then he calls Lazarus out. So the house at Bethany holds three ways of loving the same friend: Martha's work and her bold faith, Mary's listening, and Lazarus, who simply comes back to the table. The Church keeps all three on one day now. Not the busy one against the quiet one. A household.
screen: `MARTHA, MARTHA.` · `SHE OPENED THE DOOR.` · `SHE GOES OUT TO MEET HIM.` · `THREE WAYS OF LOVING ONE FRIEND.` · then, large: `JESUS WEPT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set a place in your mind. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you could welcome this week. A friend you haven't seen. A neighbor. Someone new in town. Picture them at your table. Now notice the Martha in you, already planning what to cook and whether the house is clean enough. Let that go for a moment and be Mary: just glad they're there, listening. If you pray, you can ask God to bless that table. If you don't, simply hold the person in mind until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Martha. The sister of Mary and Lazarus in Bethany, who welcomed Jesus into her house, worried over the serving, and went out to meet him with bold faith.
Your line: the house at bethany. Today, host a friend, or set a date to. Keep the meal simple, and sit down with them. Day one thousand twelve.

1013.title: Peter Chrysologus (30 July)
1013.hook: golden-worded bishop of Ravenna known for short sermons
1013.tomorrow: Our Lady of the Snows (5 August)
1013.howItsDone: Catholics may keep the optional memorial of Saint Peter Chrysologus on 30 July, and a sermon attributed to him on prayer, fasting and mercy is read in the Liturgy of the Hours during Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Martha, Mary and Lazarus, the household at Bethany. Your line was the house at bethany. Who will you welcome to your table? Day one thousand thirteen.

A sermon that ends while people are still paying attention. Not the homily that circles the runway before it lands. Today's saint aimed for the first kind. He was a bishop in the Italian city of Ravenna, he preached often, and tradition remembers him for keeping it short, so his people wouldn't tire and lose the thread. Somewhere along the way he was given a second name, a nickname that stuck so well it replaced his own. Today, the bishop with the golden word.
screen: `A SERMON THAT ENDS IN TIME.` → `A BISHOP OF RAVENNA.` → `A NICKNAME THAT STUCK.`

segments.voice: His name was Peter. Chrysologus came later. It's Greek, and tradition says it means golden-worded, a title given for the way he spoke. Sermons under his name have come down to us, and they are brief. One idea, opened up, and done. A line from the wisdom books fits him. In the Douay-Rheims, Ecclesiastes says: "therefore let thy words be few." The verse gives its reason just before: God is in heaven, and you are on earth. Few words aren't a lack of things to say. They're a kind of respect, for God and for the person listening. One of the sermons attributed to him is still read in the Church's prayer during Lent. It ties three practices together: prayer, fasting and mercy. In his picture they belong to each other and shouldn't be pulled apart. Prayer knocks, fasting obtains, mercy receives. If you pray but never show mercy, he says in effect, you've cut the thread. He fits a lot into a small space. That's the gift of a short word: it has to carry weight, so you choose it carefully. The Church honors him as a teacher of the faith, and a whole teaching is folded into his nickname. Say what is true, say it well, and stop. Gold is heavy. A little goes a long way.
screen: `PETER, THEN CHRYSOLOGUS.` · `ONE IDEA, AND DONE.` · `PRAYER, FASTING, MERCY TOGETHER.` · `SAY IT WELL, THEN STOP.` · then, large: `THEREFORE LET THY WORDS BE FEW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one short, true sentence. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you need to say something to. Maybe it's thank you. Maybe it's sorry, or I'm proud of you, or I'm worried. Now cut it down. No speech, no explanation. Just the sentence, as few words as it can hold. Turn it over until it's simple and true. If you pray, you can offer God a short word too, as few words as you like. If you don't, simply rest in the quiet after the sentence. The bell holds the time.
Peter Chrysologus. A bishop of Ravenna whose short sermons earned him a Greek nickname that tradition says means golden-worded.
Your line: short and golden. Today, say your one short, true sentence to the person it's for, and then stop talking. Day one thousand thirteen.

1014.title: Our Lady of the Snows (5 August)
1014.hook: Rome's great basilica of Mary, founded, legend says, after summer snow
1014.howItsDone: Catholics may keep the optional memorial of the Dedication of the Basilica of Saint Mary Major on 5 August, known in popular devotion as Our Lady of the Snows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter Chrysologus, the bishop of the short golden sermon. Your line was short and golden. What short, true sentence did you say? Day one thousand fourteen.

Rome in August. The stones hold the heat long after dark. Shutters are closed against the sun. And on one hilltop, the story goes, one summer morning, the ground is white. Snow. Not a dusting on a mountain far away, but snow on a hill in the middle of Rome, in the full heat of summer. People come out to stare at it. Someone takes it as a message. Today, a church that tradition says was drawn in the snow.
screen: `ROME IN AUGUST.` → `A WHITE HILLTOP.` → `SOMEONE READS A MESSAGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the legend. A Roman husband and wife have no children and want to give what they own to Mary. They pray to know how. In a dream, she tells them to build a church where snow will fall. The same night, the story says, the pope has the same dream. In the morning, snow covers part of the Esquiline hill, and the pope traces the outline of the church in it. That church is the great basilica of Saint Mary Major. So today has two names. In the Church's calendar it's the dedication of that basilica. In older and popular devotion, it's Our Lady of the Snows. And the difference is worth saying plainly: the snow is told as legend, and the feast keeps the dedication of a real building, still standing, still a place of prayer. Why keep a legend at all? Because of what it's pointing at. Snow in August is a surprise no one could plan. The psalms speak of God as the one behind the weather. In the Douay-Rheims: "Who giveth snow like wool." The legend takes that line and puts it on a Roman hill. It says: grace can come out of season, when everything around says it's impossible. At the basilica, a custom remembers the story on the feast, with white petals let fall from the ceiling during the Mass, like snow. A summer snowfall, made of flowers.
screen: `A DREAM, AND SNOW ON A HILL.` · `THE BASILICA OF SAINT MARY MAJOR.` · `A LEGEND, AND A REAL CHURCH.` · `GRACE OUT OF SEASON.` · then, large: `WHO GIVETH SNOW LIKE WOOL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch for something out of season. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last week. Was there anything you didn't expect? A kind word from someone who's usually short with you. A good day in a hard month. A small thing that went right. Find one. Hold it the way people held the snow that morning, as something to look at before you explain it away. If you pray, you can thank God for it. If you don't, just let yourself be surprised by it again. The bell holds the time.
Mary Major, the great Roman basilica behind today's other name, Our Lady of the Snows, recalling the legend of snow on a summer hill.
Your line: snow in august. Today, look for one surprise, something out of season, and when you find it, stop and look before you move on. Day one thousand fourteen.

1015.title: Pontian and Hippolytus (13 August)
1015.hook: a pope and his rival, sent to the same mines, reconciled before dying
1015.howItsDone: Catholics may keep the optional memorial of Saints Pontian and Hippolytus on 13 August, remembering them together as martyrs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Our Lady of the Snows, and a legend of summer snow on a Roman hill. Your line was snow in august. What surprise did you find? Day one thousand fifteen.

Two men on opposite sides of a split in the church at Rome. Each with his own followers. Each sure the other has it wrong. Then the empire arrests them both and ships them to the same place: the mines on the island of Sardinia, where prisoners were sent to hard labor. Same dust. Same chains. Same shortage of food and light. Whatever they argued about in Rome is very far away. Today, a pope and his rival, and what happened to the quarrel underground.
screen: `OPPOSITE SIDES OF A SPLIT.` → `ARRESTED, BOTH OF THEM.` → `THE SAME MINES.`

segments.voice: Hippolytus was a priest and a learned writer in Rome, sharp and serious. He clashed with the popes of his day over teaching and over how gently to treat sinners who wanted to come back. The split went deep enough that a group followed him as their own bishop, against the bishop of Rome. Pontian, later, was that bishop of Rome, the pope. So when the persecution came, the Church in Rome was already divided, and the empire took the two leaders of the two sides. In the mines, tradition says, two things happened. Pontian stepped down from his office, so the Church in Rome could choose a new pope and not be left without a shepherd. And Hippolytus was reconciled to the Church, and urged his followers to return to unity. Both died there, far from home. Their bodies were brought back to Rome, tradition says, and buried, and the Church has kept them together on the same day, the pope and his old rival. Jesus had said it plainly. In the Douay-Rheims: "go first to be reconciled to thy brother." Not after you win the argument. First. These two came to it late, in chains, and the Church still remembers it as peace. The Church didn't remember Hippolytus as the man who split the community. It remembers him, with Pontian, as a martyr who came home. A quarrel that lasted years ended in a mine, and the calendar still sets the two names side by side.
screen: `A PRIEST WHO SPLIT FROM ROME.` · `BOTH SENT TO SARDINIA.` · `ONE STEPS DOWN, ONE COMES BACK.` · `KEPT TOGETHER ON ONE DAY.` · then, large: `GO FIRST TO BE RECONCILED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring one rival to mind. Settle, and breathe. Not your worst enemy, just someone you've been on the other side from. A coworker. A relative. An old friend after a falling-out. Picture the two of you somewhere neither of you chose, side by side, with the argument far away. What would you say first? If you pray, you can pray for them by name, and for yourself. If you don't, simply wish them well, once, and mean it as much as you can. The bell holds the time.
Hippolytus, the priest who opposed Pope Pontian's church. Sent to the same mines, the two were reconciled there, and are honored together as martyrs.

Your line: reconciled in the mines. Seven days now: Camillus, Sharbel, James, the house at Bethany, Peter Chrysologus, the summer snow, and now two rivals at peace. Today, if an old quarrel surfaces, don't argue it again. Ask the other person one honest question about how they are. Day one thousand fifteen.

they died in Rome
both died in the mines of Sardinia. their bodies were brought back later, tradition says.

fork.setup: you're Hippolytus, in the mines, beside the pope you opposed for years. what do you do?
options: keep your distance. you were right.
be reconciled, and tell your followers to return.
say nothing and wait it out.
fork.reveal: tradition says Hippolytus was reconciled to the Church and urged his followers back to unity. he and Pontian are honored together.

trapdoor: what you thought: two martyrs who happen to share a day.
what it means: a pope and his rival, arrested together, who made peace in the mines.
what a scholar hears: Hippolytus, a learned Roman writer who led a rival community; Pontian's stepping down and their reconciliation come from tradition.

sources.ref: Traditions of Pontian and Hippolytus (Liberian Catalogue; Roman tradition)
